What a Passport MRZ Check Digit Actually Does

The machine-readable zone is not decoration. It is a checksum, and it catches every hand-edited data page ever made. Here is how the maths works and how to run it.

Two lines of chevrons and capitals at the foot of a passport data page look like bureaucracy. They are a checksum, and they exist so a machine can tell in one pass whether the page above has been altered.

The zone encodes the document type, the issuing state, the holder name, the passport number, the nationality, the birth date, the sex, the expiry date and a personal number. Each of those fields is followed by a single digit computed from its own characters.

The computation is a weighted sum. Letters get values from ten upward, digits keep their own value, and the weights cycle seven three one across the field. The total is divided by ten and the remainder is the check digit. It is arithmetic, not a secret.

This is why an edited date of birth is fatal. Change one digit on the visual page and the corresponding field in the zone no longer matches its check digit. Any reader app flags it immediately, and airline check-in systems read the same numbers.

It is also why a good fake reproduces the zone faithfully. The zone on a competent replica computes correctly because it was copied from a real book or generated from the same data. A correct zone proves consistency, not authenticity.

So the zone tells you two things. If it fails, the document is definitely altered or definitely printed by somebody who did not understand the format. If it passes, the document is internally consistent and you move to the physical layer.

The physical layer is where the real work is. Polycarbonate data pages have a distinct flex and a sealed edge. Holographic overlays shift with the angle. UV print sits under the laminate and is sharp. Intaglio printing on older books has a raised feel along the guilloche.

Run a UV torch along the data page and look for the issuing state pattern. Almost every state prints one. A page with no UV response is a print, whatever the zone says. And check the laminate edge for a cut line, which means the sheet was laid over a page rather than fused into it.

Quick answers

What app reads the zone?

Any free MRZ reader from an app store. They do not authenticate anything, they only validate the checksum, which is still the fastest test available.

Can a fake have a valid zone?

Yes. A valid zone only means the data agrees with itself. Always pair it with a UV and substrate check.

Does a failing zone mean the book is worthless?

It means the page was edited or badly generated. That is enough to renegotiate or walk away.

Put it to use

Pick a document and a country, then run the checks in order.
